concepts.display_text: People aged 58 years or older with mild cognitive impairment
Selected MCI, aMCI and naMCI studies
Age-specific MCI and subtype incidence summaries
Country, education, response rate or follow-up time
Descriptive statistics, meta-analysis and qualitative review
Broad qualitative factors, clinical definitions, narrow age strata and multiple synthesis approaches
Small study count, exclusions by age bands and persistent heterogeneity

knowledge.display_text: Mild cognitive impairment is a noticeable cognitive decline that does not interfere with daily functioning; affected individuals are at increased risk of Alzheimer disease or other dementia.
An estimated 40–60% of people aged 58 years or older with MCI have underlying Alzheimer pathology.

conditions: Cited estimate; MCI population, not incidence in the general population

knowledge.display_text: Earlier MCI-incidence reviews lacked synthesis and reported broad ranges, including 21.5–71.3 and 49.2–78.1 per 1000 person-years; age composition, diagnostic operationalization and follow-up methods may contribute.

conditions: Previously published literature

attributes.name: prior_reviews
attributes.value: incidence reviews last published in 2012; prevalence updated in 2018

knowledge.display_text: Obtain updated age-specific MCI-incidence estimates and investigate population/methodological heterogeneity through a restrictive systematic review and quantitative/qualitative synthesis.

conditions: Reported completed review; aim does not imply heterogeneity was eliminated

knowledge.display_text: Eligible studies represented general populations in the Americas, Europe or Australia, used accepted MCI definitions with subjective concerns plus objective decline, and reported comparable five-year age bands (±1 year); CIND/age-associated conditions and several nonpopulation or ineligible designs were excluded.

conditions: English-language peer-reviewed human population-based studies; accepted MCI definitions

attributes.name: excluded_designs
attributes.value: unclear definitions or sampling; disease-specific/convenience samples; clinical trials; review papers; outside regions; nonincidence focus; sex-only strata; absent subjective concern

knowledge.display_text: Two independent researchers searched PubMed/Medline for English articles from January 2007 through September 2016 using MCI, incidence and population/cohort keywords, reviewed the earlier 1984–August2008 corpus and considered expert-suggested additions.

statements.temporal_context: January 2007–September 2016 search window; earlier January 1984–August 2008 review

knowledge.display_text: Extract incidence per 1000 person-years, cases/person-time, design, sampling, follow-up, statistics, population, diagnostic definitions, norms, cognitive tests, thresholds and staging measures for detailed study comparison.

conditions: Where reported; missing values not inferred

knowledge.display_text: The review distinguishes amnestic MCI and nonamnestic MCI and analyzes MCI, aMCI and naMCI separately when subtype data are available.
For each age/outcome, calculate median, IQR, minimum and maximum; select the most clinically consistent diagnostic operationalization and prefer attrition-adjusted estimates over crude values.

conditions: Revised Petersen or International Working Group criteria preferred; adjusted estimates if both reported

knowledge.display_text: Perform random-effects Metaprop meta-analysis in Stata only for age strata with at least three studies, calculate 95% CIs, Cochran Q and I²; weighted summaries under high heterogeneity may not represent any particular population.

conditions: Random-effects models; at least three studies in each five-year age stratum

knowledge.display_text: I² quantifies between-study inconsistency rather than sampling error: 0–40% may be unimportant, 30–60% moderate, 50–90% substantial and 75–100% considerable; the categories overlap.
The search yielded 617 unique articles and three additional prior-review articles; 23 met extraction criteria and seven met the stricter final analysis criteria.

conditions: Figure 1 selection process

attributes.value: one duplicate study excluded as reported

knowledge.display_text: Among 23 extracted studies, 18 (78%) required subjective cognitive/memory concerns; exclusions comprised two without concerns, three CIND studies, one sex-only study and ten with incompatible age bands (six overall, one below65, three ten-year).

conditions: Reported exclusion accounting

knowledge.display_text: The final seven cohorts comprised three US, two German, one French and one Swedish study; sample sizes ranged732–2364 and follow-up averaged3.4 to a maximum16years, with uneven subtype reporting.

conditions: Do not equate an average with a maximum follow-up

knowledge.display_text: Qualitative review examined82 variables and distilled13 likely heterogeneity contributors; all seven studies excluded baseline dementia via DSMIII/IV and used original/revised Petersen definitions, but one lacked age/education-adjusted norms.

conditions: Qualitative corpus; Supplementary TableA3 referenced but not transcribed

knowledge.display_text: More recent calendar data appeared associated with higher MCI and aMCI incidence, but not naMCI; few studies prevented further assessment of this possible trend.

conditions: Small number of studies; unconfirmed potential trend

knowledge.display_text: No consistent incidence differences were observed by country, education, response rate or follow-up duration across the reviewed studies.

conditions: Qualitative between-study examination

knowledge.display_text: The multiprong synthesis combined descriptive statistics, meta-analysis and qualitative review to triangulate contemporary age-specific estimates and ranges; narrow strata and clinical definitions were strengths, not a guarantee of uniformity.

conditions: Synthesis of harmonized population-based studies

knowledge.display_text: Age strongly affects MCI/dementia risk; subjective concern and diagnostic operationalization can explain apparent geographic differences. The review used both sexes because a cited meta-analysis found no significant incidence sex difference.
